Bathers at Coney Island Object to Their Presence in the Water.
NEW YORK, July 30.—An attempt was made to lynch two negroes at Coney Island today because they wanted to bathe in the ocean with the white men and women. Bryant Teal and Frank Davis, the negroes, had narrow escapes.

They slipped into bathing suits during the heat of the day and went to the head of the pier. About sixty white men and women were in the water at the time. An outcry against the presence of the negroes was raised by some one.

Several men grabbed Davis, who is slight of build, and pulled him out into deep water. They did not know that he could swim, and their object seemed to drown him. Davis was pulled beyond his depth, but he proved a good and fast swimmer, and saved himself by striking out and away from the whites, who seemed to want his life. He made a wide detour, got to shore and ran for cover.

In the meantime Teal, who stands six feet tall and is of powerful build, had gotten to shore and taken to flight under a hail of stones. The crowd took after him. Teal was almost winded when a white man named James Beaver saw his plight and called him into his little place of business.

Beaver stood off the crowd while Teal hid in the rear until he got his wind again. Then he slipped out of a back window and continued his flight until he was safely home. In the chase after Teal so much excitement was created that a dozen calls for the police were sent in.

Negroes Threatened with Lynching.
A telegram from New York on Friday said:

An attempt was made to lynch two negroes at Coney Island to-day. The attempt was made because they wanted to bathe in the ocean with white men and women. They had narrow escapes.

When they appeared on the beach about sixty women were in the water. A cry against the presence of the negroes was raised. One of them was grabbed and pulled into deep water with the object of drowning him, but he was a good swimmer and got away. The other one also made for shore and both were chased and stoned until they got away. Several extra calls for police were sent out.

DIAZ REFUSES.
President Diaz of Mexico has refused to accept the life-membership tendered him by the International Negro-nating Sunday School Congress.

President Diaz says: "When a people like the Americans draw the colorline on black people and I accept membership, with my republic full of colored people, who are in our army, manning our railroads and engaged in all the natural industries, I would be unfit to be the head of the nation. The black man has rights and privileges in Mexico which the world must respect and I will not soil my hands by accepting membership in an association which would degrade my fellowman. I trust that the American Negro will not weaken, but will fight for his rights until the end."

Charles D. Norton, Secretary to the President, is a great success in his new place. He has tact and skill and succeeds in pleasing all who have business with the Chief Executive.

WHITE MAN'S OCEAN.

But He Is Strangely Inconsistent in Enforcing His Claim to the Water.

The Caucasians of Coney Island are becoming very sensitive on the race question. They have taken to objecting—violently—to the use of their ocean by Negroes. "Go swimming in the Dead sea or Great Salt lake or the Gowanus canal if you got to bathe," they told two black men who had the ternity last Friday to approach the Atlantic for a wash, "but keep away from us."

Then with curious inconsistency they proceeded to throw them into this same Atlantic and half drown them, and by this action, on their own statements, poluted the water for Caucasian use. Sweet reasonableness should have led them to form a cordon along the sands and guard their ocean from the dark skins at all hazards. "God must needs laugh outright could such a thing be," said Caryle, "to see his wondrous manikins here below." In this case it would be a bitter laugh, with much of shame mixed in—New York Globe.

Just a Mid-Summer Suggestion.
Just by way of a suggestlon, why wouldn't it be a good idea for the city council to look up the record and find out how many and what spur tracks, for which franchises have been granted during the past several years, are now owned by the L. & N. railroad?

It appears that a Pensacola wholesale firm recently applied for and was granted a franchise to construct a spur track down to one of its warehouses near the bay front. Before the L. & N. would build the track, however, it develops that the wholesale firm had to assign the franchise over to the railroad company. It also still further develops that the franchise calls for a great deal more track than the wholesale firm has any use for, but the track does give the L. & N. another line direct to the water front.

An investigation will probably show that the L. & N. owns all of the franchises which have ever been granted to individuals in Pensacola for the building of spur tracks.

Yet with all of this, the railroad company today refuses to deliver freight to coast steamship lines even though these franchise grants enable it to place cars within 20 feet of the steamship company's private docks. Freight for steamers has to be unloaded from the L. & N. cars at points remote from the water front and hauled by team down to the steamer wharves simply because the L. & N. wants to make the handling of this freight just as costly and as burdensome and as annoying to the steamship people as it can possibly make it.

Aside from the interests of the railroad company and the steamship companies there is still a bigger interest—the public welfare. It is high time now, before any more spur track franchises are granted, that the public interests be looked into. The city council can do that much, and the interstate commerce commission should look into the discrimination that exists by virtue of the grants already made.

In the meantime, suppose we get a list of all such franchises that were originally granted to, and ostensibly for the use of, private individuals and see just how much of a monopoly the L. & N. has in the matter. The franchise committee of the city council can easily do this and The Journal will take exceeding delight in publishing its report.

BAY MINETTE.
New Industry Being Established at Stockton.

Bay Minette, Aug. 8.—(Special)—The case of Mrs. Missouri Phillips vs. L. D. Parkton was tried before Judge J. H. H. Smith today.

Another business enterprise which promises to rival that of the tobacco industry and a plant which will surpass the tobacco curing plant in size, is giving employment to more than 100 men at Stockton, a town about ten miles north of here on the Tensaw river. The Bacon-Underwod Veneer Company is constructing a mammoth plant on the banks of the river.

Some time ago the company purchased about 10,000 acres of hardwood timber land lying along the river and laid plans for its development. Their plans include a mammoth cement block mill, two large dry kilns and a spacious dry shed and a goodly number of other out buildings. This morning the force of men in the employ of the company began preparing the ground for the dry kilns. The mill proper will be seventy-five feet wide and 150 feet long and will be constructed of cement, even to the roof which will be covered with concrete slab. The two large dry kilns each will be seventy-five feet in width and 150 feet long. The dry shed will cover nearly an acre of ground.

Fully 150 men will be employed when the mill is running and most of these will take up residences in Stockton. A new mercantile store has been opened by O. W. Byrne and Dr. J. H. Hastie and new life has been assumed by the once apparently dead town. The town is on the river and Mobile is in easy reach. Mobile will also be the market for the products of the plant. Several launches are being constructed for the company which will ply along the river. The total cost of the plant when complete will reach about $50,000.

Miss Annie Lounse Staats of Mobile,

who has been visiting at the home of Frank Stone, returned to her home this morning.

A. B. Cromartie of Wilmer was a visitor in town Sunday.

Agnau Stapleton of Dothan is the guest of friends.

Mrs. F. I. Dinwiddle, postmistress, made a business trip to Mobile today.

MARION EXCITED OVER
ATTEMPT BY ASSASSIN

Marlon, Aug. 8.—(Special.)—Calhoun Watters, night watchman, was shot in the neck by an unknown person about 4:30 o'clock Sunday morning. The shot came from a shot gun and from an upstairs window in the King House.

Walters had a difficulty with General Moore, a negro, the night before, and had been warned to keep on his guard. In making his rounds he kept well in the streets until the hour he was shot, when in company with Jake Hopper he started to his home along the sidewalk by the hotel.

Medical attention was at once rendered and it was found the officer was dangerously wounded in the neck with bird shot. Considerable excitement was created and citizens from the country were coming and going all day and at one time it looked as if a lynching might occur. General Moore and his father, General Moore, Sr., negroes, and Tom Sullivan, also a negro, were immediately arrested and placed in jail and kept well guarded.

The fact that the fall term Circuit Court convened today, and Judge Miller's arrival Sunday evening had much to do towards quieting the crowd. It has already been ascertained that General Moore, Jr., was seen on the streets at 1 o'clock Saturday night.

Walters lived in East Perry until accepting the position of night watchman about eighteen months ago. He was assistant doorkeeper to the House during the administration of Governor Oates.

The store of Mrs. E. H. Purifoy, located near the depot, was broken into and robbed Saturday night. There is no clue to the guilty parties. This store was entered several months ago, a small iron safe carried about 100 yards away, dynamited and rifled of several hundred dollars. The loss this time was small.

MARION RECOVERS FROM EXCITEMENT
CITIZENS ARE APPARENTLY WILLING TO ALLOW THE LAW TO TAKE ITS COURSE WITH NEGRO WOULD-BE ASSASSINS
Marion, August 8.—(Special.)—Marion is comparatively quiet today after the excitement caused yesterday by the attempt to assassinate Officer Watters. The fall term of Perry county circuit convened this morning, and the first work of the grand jury was the investigation of the attempt made early Sunday morning to assassinate Policeman Watters. Sufficient evidence was secured by the sheriff's department on Sunday to show that a conspiracy had been formed by a band of lawless negroes to assassinate the officers. Two negroes are in jail here.

Rumors of the probable lynching of the entre band were heard throughout the day Sunday, but no demonstration was made. It is the opinion of many persons that the people were willing to trust the matter to the courts, as the citizens of the county have great confidence in the integrity of Judge Miller, and believe he, with Solicitor Thompson, will immediately use the power of their offices to give speedy trial to the accused negroes.

The town officials will aid the state in solving the crime, as Policeman Watters is known to have knowledge of a great amount of the lawlessness that has been shown around Marion during the past six months.

The First district Sunday school convention held at Mount Nebo church at the close of last week was largely attended, and reports from various churches show the interest in this work increasing in the district. The Second district convention will be held at Helberger next Saturday.

W. B. Alexander of Felix has rented the W. T. Harris home, at the corner of Bibb and LaFayette streets, and will move his family to Marion September 1.

Robert E. Lee will move his family to Florida on September 1.

Cotton sold here on Saturday for 15 cents. One lot, covering three annual crops, was closed out at this price.

DAVIS DIES OF WOUNDS.
Fugitive Lived Until Sunday Morning—Body Identified.
Orangeburg, August 28.—The body of a negro, said to be Charles Davis, the alleged slayer of Lucy Dwight, colored, near Bowman, about two weeks ago, lies dead at the county jail here this morning, the cause of the death being, as testified to by Dr. T. C. Doyle, who examined the body, gun shot wounds, two of which are seen on the body, one in the stomach and one in the left breast. The man was brought here last night by Sheriff Salley from Denmark, where he was captured yesterday as a prisoner by Magistrate Ray's constable and a posse.

He was arrested under the proclamation of Governor Ansel as Charles Davis, but had assumed, it is said, the name of Mitchell. When the sheriff arrived at Denmark, he found Davis, or Mitchell, so badly wounded that he did not attempt to remove him until advised by a physician that it was safe to do so. The wounded negro was then placed on a cot and brought here on the Southern train at 8 o'clock and put in the jail and made as comfortable as circumstances admitted, and died this morning at 8:30 o'clock.

The coroner was at once notified and a jury of inquest was organized, with J. C. Kennerly as foreman, and viewed the body and heard some testimony. Dr. Doyle testified that death was due to the wounds noted, and Sheriff Salley gave a short history of the charge held against Davis and his official connection with the prisoner since taking him in charge yesterday at Denmark. Mr. Salley stated that one Davis was wanted for murder and that the Governor had by his proclamation, declared Davis a fugitive from justice and offered a reward for his capture, and that under this proclamation the arrest had been made. He knew none of the attending circumstances. The sheriff said the prisoner had made no statement and had not talked at all. It is said, however, that the negro had admitted his identity. One or two other witnesses were put up for the purpose of identifying the body as that of Charles Davis, but as their testimony was not fully satisfactory to the jury, an adjournment was taken until late this afternoon, when others who knew Davis were examined. QUICK SHOOTING IN SOUTH.
Mississippi Leads Other States in Rapid-fire Homicides.
From the Chicago' Inter Ocean. A dispatch from Elliott.

From the Chicago' Inter Ocean.

A dispatch from Elliott, Miss., tells of the remarkable shooting record made by Deputy Sheriff Sid Cauley, of Carroll County. In about ten seconds he killed five men and wounded two.

The dead and wounded are all negroes, who were not only resisting arrest, but were advancing on the deputy with axes and pitchforks with the avowed intention of cutting him down.

They had made the sheriff "take to the woods" the day before, and apparently expected to do the same with the deputy. But they failed to take into account his proficiency with a gun.

This exhibition of skill, which has never been exceeded even in a Bret Harte short story, calls attention to an interesting fact. This is that Mississippi has never got the credit it deserves as a sharpshooting State.

Everybody hears a good deal about "bloody Breathitt" and certain portions of Tennessee, and the readiness with which lives are snuffed out even now down on the Rio Grande. In point of fact, none of them can equal Mississippi's record in rapid-fire homicide.

The customary Mississippi affair is seldom one of those tame Texas-Kentucky-Tennessee encounters in which one man shoots another man, and, likely as not, even fails to kill the single party to whom he is devoting his attention.

There are generally several persons engaged, and it may be stated without the slightest fear of successful contradiction that the proportions of deaths to survivals is uniformly larger than in any other State in the Union.

Within the past fifteen years there have been in Mississippi several pretty stiff affairs in small towns, participated in by four persons. Each principal in each case has been aided and abetted by a relative or personal friend. The score at the end of every one of these affairs, according to the writer's information, has generally been as follows: Dead, 3; wounded, 1; total, 4.

In point of fact, Mississippi is the only State which the careful student of informal rapid-fire homicide naturally thinks of as the scene of the tremendous mortality referred to in the late John Hay's ballad of the "Whisky Skin:"

They piled the bodies around the door:
There must have been a cord or more.
Girls went that winter, as a rule,
Alone to singin' school.

And yet the rare effectiveness of Mississippi shooting is seldom commented on by newspapers and special publications that are generally disposed to give honor where honor is due. Of course, the total of homicides is greater in several other States. But the percentage of deaths in a single affray in Mississippi is as large as it is unrecognized.

The only explanation of this singular neglect is that Mississippi is simply suffering the usual penalty of quiet, unobtrusive thoroughness. It has not advertised itself properly, and has thus let other States reap the honor that it alone deserves as a dead-shot Commonwealth.

Three Men Wounded by Negroes in Douglas Club.
WHITES STARTED BATTLE
One Hit Woman with Bottle and General Melee Resulted—
One Said To Be Dying.
Three white men were shot in the Douglas Club, at No. 147 West 28th street, a negro resort, shortly after midnight this morning, when they started a free fight with about a hundred negroes. Two of the men were so seriously wounded that they were taken to the New York Hospital in a critical condition. The reserves of the West 30th street station were called out to stay the riot, which was then in full swing.

Shortly before midnight four taxicabs drove up to the entrance of the club and about a dozen white men clambered out, shouting lustily and showing evidence of having passed an enjoyable night. They all marched into the club and took seats about the tables. The Douglas Club is one of the most frequented resorts of its kind in the Tenderloin.

The white men were conspicuous by the noise they made, and several times clashes between them and negroes were narrowly averted. The crisis arrived when one of the visiting brigade picked up a heavy whiskey bottle and aimed with unwavering hand at the head of a young negro woman who was singing. The bottle struck the singer on the head. This method of showing displeasure was bitterly resented by every negro in the room, and it served as the spark to touch off the smouldering fire.

Immediately the negro men and women were on their feet, shouting and crying for revenge. Bottles, glasses, chairs and everything of a movable nature was soon gyrating through the smoke laden atmosphere, and the generally accepted rule in vogue seemed to be, "When you see a head, hit it." The rule was followed out with varied success, but when the negroes tired of this form of diversion they dug down into their pockets for razors and revolvers.

The scene now resembled a battlefield, and the hoarse shouts of men and women and the crash of breaking mirrors and overturned tables were interspersed with the sharp reports of exploding cartridges. The air became so thick with gunpowder that it was difficult to see ten feet away, and then it was that men began to drop on the floor, suffering from bullet wounds.

The cries of the fighting men and women were carried out to the street, causing a large crowd to gather. Every little while an eddy of revolver smoke would be wafted through a broken window pane, and the whole interior seemed to be a modern inferno.

When the whites realized that their forces were being rapidly thinned and that they were in the centre of a black hornets' nest, they began to back toward the doors, carrying their wounded from the field. Three men were bundled into the waiting taxi-cabs when it was seen that their wounds might prove serious, and were rushed through the streets to the New York Hospital.

John McCarthy, an agent, of No. 136 Sixth avenue, and Joseph Cryons, of No. 496 Hudson avenue, both were shot in the right side and arm. They were unconscious and were at once placed on the operating table. The third man laid low by a bullet was William Dehriens, of No. 500 East 137th street, who was shot in the left arm.

Just as the wounded men were hustled away to the hospital Captain O'Brien, of the West 30th street station, at the head of the reserves, came running down the street and stormed the smoking citadel. They broke down the doors and cleared the place. They then arrested Edmund Johnson, the alleged proprietor of the place, and Frank H. Berryman, of No. 329 West 39th street, both negroes. They were charged with felonious assault and locked up, after they had been identified at the hospital by McCarthy and Cryons.

Chicago, Ill., Sept. 19—Stephen Green, the negro charged with killing a Mr. Sidel at Jericho. Ark., and who was arrested here several weeks ago on a fugitive warrant, was ordered discharged from custody by Judge Tuthill today. The court based his action on the technicality that Green was not named in the indictment as the murderer. According to Green's story, he and Mr. Sidel quarreled and began shooting at each other. Green was nearly out of the state, being taken back to the Arkansas, when the officers in charge were ordered by telegraph to bring the prisoner back to Chicago on a writ of habeis corpus.

Green declared that he could not get a fair trial in Arkansas.

Negro Accused of Killing Man in Arkansas Discharged by Chicago Judge.
Sheriff Fred D. Nellis rereived the following message from Chicago yesterday:

"Steve Green discharged by Judge Tuthill after full hearing today.

"ANDERSON & WRIGHT."

Steve Green is the negro who was charged with killing a planter at Jericho, Ark., and who was captured at Chicago several weeks ago, and a requisition was made upon Governor Deneen by the governor of Arkansas for his return to that state. The requisition was granted and the negro in custody of an Arkansas deputy sheriff was brought as far south as Cairo, where the sheriff of Cook county telegraphed Sheriff Nellis to head the prisoner off and return him to Chicago, which Sheriff Nellis did, the excuse for this action being that there was fear that the negro would be lynched on his arrival at the scene of his crime.
By the action of Judge Tuthill Steve Green is a free man as far as the state of Illinois is concerned. If he goes out of the state the Arkansas authorities will have a right to ask for a requisition from the governor of the state in which he is found.

D., July 31.—(Special Telegram.)—The shooting and wounding of a policeman by a negro, the wounding of a special officer and finally the killing of the negro by a well-directed shot from the revolver of another policeman were events which kept the central part of the city in a state of excitement until an early hour this morning.

About 1,000 men assisted in the search for the negro after the commencement of the trouble, many of them demanding that he be lynched if caught. Pleading on the part of local officers and the cooler heads among the mob prevented an attack being made on the homes of inoffensive negroes.

Sioux Falls, Aug. 1.—Saturday night James Collins and Martin Ellingson, police officers, were shot and wounded by Wm. Brown, colored, who resisted arrest. The negro was later shot and instantly killed by officer Herman Weins.

J. A. Fowler was with officer Collins at the time he was shot, and made the following statement in regard to the affair:

"The whole trouble started in Henry Levinger's saloon. I was in the saloon in company with a young fellow who works for Donahue Bros. The colored man came into the saloon and my friend in a joking way walked after the colored man close to his heels and when the fellom saw him it made him mad. He called us all manner of ugly names. We did not care to get into trouble with him so said nothing in reply. He went out and stood in front of the saloon looking in at us. After a while we went out and when we passed by the Cataract hotel on Ninth street he was there in company with six other negroes and there was a hack there. They all got in. This was about 8.30. He started toward us again and drew a revolver. We got away and I asw office Collins and told him about it. He said a warrant should be gotten out for his arrest. We went south on Phillips avenue to a saloon opposite Joe Tossini's store and there were some fellows there in a quarrel. I then caught sight of the colored man and pointed him out to Collins. Collins caught hold of him and the colored fellow resisted and the officer partly threw him to the ground. In getting up the colored man broke loose and whipped out his revolver and fired. Collins grabbed him again but the fellow stepped back and fired again. That shot missed. I then jumped on the colored man's back and caught hold of the arm in which hand he held the revolver. Quick as a flash he changed the gun to the other hand and fired again. He was evidently after me with that shot. He then ran across the street and I saw Officer Johnson and I said there goes the man you want. He started after him and I followed but the fellow was too fast for us and he soon disappeared in the darkness."

The second shooting occurred not far from the Queen Bee mill, near some cars on the Illinois Central track. Martin Ellingson, a former police of Deadwood, was sworn in as a special officer and in company with Ray-Nelson, had been down to Sam Wortham's place near the packing house where the negro Brown had boarded, to search for the fugitive. They came back up the track to look among some box cars and met the negro. They tried to stop him, but the negro started to run. Elingson drew his revolver and fired several times. The negro turned and fired one shot which struck Ellingson in the leg about six inches above the knee. Then for the second time he made his escape.

It was about one o'clock when Officer Herman Weins, who was crouching on the watch near an out building near the Sam Wortham place, heard a step at his left and looking around saw a figure in the darkness. Weins immediately turned his flash light on the man and looked into the barrel of a revolver. The bullet entered the negro's forehead over the left eye, killing him instantly.

This poor pay has often been due to ignorance on the part of the printers themselves and if this move for education puts the business on a paying basis many a poor printer will rejoice.

President Taft has sent Senator Murray Crane on a trip of inspection of the middle west to ascertain the true political situation. Mr. Crane will travel around and visit with the prominent stand pat leaders in each state and return to President Taft and report that there is no insurgency worth mentioning but that all the stand pat candidates will be reelected by increased majorities. And Taft will believe him provided he does not read any papers.

After a near riot a negro was shot in Sioux Falls Saturday night by a police officer. The trouble started in a saloon when a "smart" white man mimiced the negro. Two things are brought out by the affair. One is that the trouble was entirely due to the saloons and the liquor sold in them. The other is that it was the white man who first provoked the negro. Fortunately the state escaped the disgrace of a lynching but the saloons are still doing business and the trouble is being made an excuse for the further pestering of the blacks by the whites.

Instead the buck rake brings in the hay and the stacker carries it aloft to the stack or if the hay is meant for the barn the automatic loader puts it on the wagon as the team walks across the field and the harpoon fork stows it away in the barn. DESPERATE NEGRO SLAIN BY OFFICER WOUNDS A SIOUX FALLS POLICE OFFICER AND DEPUTY AND LATER IS KILLED IN GUN FIGHT WITH POLICEMAN
One police officer shot and dangerously wounded, a special officer seriously injured by a shot in the leg, a thousand men searching the town for the negro who did the shooting and finally, the killing of the negro by a shot from the revolver of another policeman, are the chief points in a tragedy which caused great excitement in Sioux Falls last night.

The shooting occurred as the result of the attempt of Officer Collins to arrest a negro by the name of William Brown, who had flashed a revolver in an altercation with some young men in front of the Levinger saloon at about 10 o'clock. The arrest was attempted in front of the dye works, opposite Tossini's store, on Phillips avenue. The negro drew a gun and shot Collins in the body just below the heart, and then made his escape, running south on Phillips avenue.

With the smoking pistol still in his hand the crazed negro started on a dead run up to Eleventh street on Phillips avenue, on Eleventh street he turned, going as far as Main avenue, where he went into the alley and was lost in the darkness.

Excited people who had seen the shooting stood still and watched the negro escape and it was several moments before the crowd was calmed down enough to start in pursuit. The first thing that the men thought of was that the colored man was armed and they lost some time in the efforts to get arms and several started who were not armed tramping down the grass and the weeds in the hope that they would find the man who shot "old Jim Collins."
After searching the outbuildings the crowd started out on South Main and when as far as the All Saints school, where a servant girl, Ester Myrseth, employed at the home of B. S. McMahon, said that she had seen a colored man pass by and that he had shot twice at her. Rumors then started that he was hiding in the All Saints school which is now vacant, so the mob armed with shot guns, rifles and pistols searched over the grounds of the school threatening to hang "the nigger," if they should find him.

People in that neighborhood, who are the owners of autos, filled them up with members of the mob and started on the road to Harrisburg and the road between this and that city was lined with automobiles until at a late hour last night, the word was received that the negro that was wanted had been shot by a special policeman near the packing plant north of town.

Collected on the corner of Eleventh street and Phillips avenue at 1:00 o'clock this morning there was a large mob armed with whatever they could get their hands on and hoping that they would be the lucky one who would have a "crack at the coon."

SHOT SPECIAL OFFICER.

The second shooting occurred not far from the Queen Bee mill, near some cars on the Illinois Central track. Martin Ellingson, a former chief of police of Deadwood, was sworn in as a special officer and in company with Ray Nelson had been down to Sam Wortham's place near the packing house where the negro Brown, had boarded, to search for the fugitive. They came back up the track to look among some box cars and met the negro. They tried to stop him, but the negro started to run. Ellingson drew his revolver and fired several times. The negro turned and fired one shot which struck Ellingson in the leg about six inches above the knee. Then for the second time he made his escape.

A QUICK SHOT.

It was about 1 o'clock when Officer Herman Weins, who was crouching on the watch near an out building near the Sam Wortham's house, heard a step at his left and looking around saw a figure in the darkness. Weins immediately turned his flash light on the man and looked into the barrel of a revolver. The revolver was snapped but missed fire, just as Weins brought his own gun into play and took a quick shot at his assailant. The bullet entered the negro's forehead over the left eye, killing him instantly.

Sam Wortham, at whose place the negro Brown, boarded, identified the body as that of William Brown and James Fowler, who was with Officer Collins when he tried to make the arrest, also saw the body and said there was no doubt but that the right negro had met his death from the bullet of Officer Weins.

THREATS OF LYNCHING.

During the hours from the time the shooting occurred until the negro was killed; there was a great crowd on the street, and threats of lynching if the negro was caught, were made. At one time the crowd surged down to the county jail believing that the negro had been captured and was imprisoned there. Sheriff Nelson assured the crowd that the man they wanted was not there, but they were not satisfied until they had taken a look through the jail.

STONES THROWN.

Later on a crowd collected on Eleventh street near the First avenue corner, where is a house occupied by colored people. Some threats were made and a few stones were thrown at the house, but officers finally induced the crowd to disperse.

During the early part of the night a number of special police were sworn in and did good work in preventing serious disorder.

The negro, Brown, who seriously wounded the two officers before being himself killed, has been in the city about two months. He has been working at the packing plant part of the time. He claimed to be an ex-United States soldier. That he was a desperate character, there is no doubt. The fact that he was sneaking up on Officer Weins with drawn revolver while the latter was watching near the Wortham place, showed that he intended to "get" as many policemen as possible before being killed or captured.

It is not believed the demonstration against the peaceable colored population of the city had any serious intent. As soon as the crowd learned that the man they were after, was killed, they went home quietly.

THE WOUNDED OFFICERS.

Officer James Collins, who was shot down while in the performance of his duty, was resting quietly at the city hospital when last heard from at 3 o'clock this morning. The bullet from the revolver of the negro entered below the heart and is supposed to have glanced around the body outside the ribs and out at the back. If the bullet went straight through the lung was not touched and it is not believed the wound is dangerous.

Collins was able to walk with assistance to Kreiser's drug store on the corner, and was then hurried to the hospital.

Ellingson's wound is painful and serious enough to lay him up for some time.

OFFICER MAIMED Sioux Falls Police Officer Shot by Negro Will Lose Limb Sioux Falls, Sept. 28.—That Martin Ellingson, former city marshal of the city of Deadwood, who was shot in the right thigh by William Brown, the negro, on the evening of Saturday, July 30, last, will have to submit to the amputation of his right foot and may possibly suffer to a greater extent, is the statement of Dr. A. Zetlitz, one of the surgeons who has been attending Ellingson since the fateful night, nearly two months ago, when Brown shot officer James Collins and Mr. Ellingson, who was acting as special policeman, before Brown himself was killed by Officer Herman
Weins, early in the morning of Sunday, July 31.

Ellingson is still a patient at Sioux Falls hospital and his right foot is so badly decomposed, as the result of severing the main artery in the right limb, by the bullet from the negro's pistol that Dr. Zetlitz stated to a reporter for The Press yesterday, that an amputation would be absolutely necessary to save Ellingson's life, and that the operation would be performed just as quickly as the line of demarkation in the limb, showing how far toward the trunk of the body the decomposition had progressed, could be determined.

Ellingson's wound, when first in inflicted, was regarded as much less serious than that of Officer Collins, who was shot by the same negro. on the same night, near the heart.

Mr. Collins, however, is up and about, has been visiting friends in Sioux City, and will return to his beat about the first of October.
